schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

content.content:
1	# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform
2	
3	Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).
4	
5	## Architecture
6	
7	- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
8	- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
9	- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
10	- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
11	- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
12	- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).
13	
14	## Portals & design system
15	
16	**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.
17	
18	- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
19	  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
20	  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
21	  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).
22	
23	- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
24	  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
25	  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
26	  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).
27	
28	- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
29	  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
30	  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
31	  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
32	  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
33	  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
34	  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
35	  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.
36	
37	- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
38	- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
39	- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).
40	
41	## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session
42	
43	`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.
44	
45	1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
46	2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
47	3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
48	4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
49	5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.
50	
51	If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).
52	
53	## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)
54	
55	- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
56	- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
57	- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.
58	
59	## Conventions
60	
61	- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
62	- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
63	- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
64	- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
65	- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
66	- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
67	- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.
68	
69	## Documentation — keep it current (required)
70	
71	- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
72	- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
73	- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
74	- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.
75	
76	## Commands
77	
78	- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
79	- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
80	- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
81	- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
82	- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
83	- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`
84	
85	## Domains & TLS
86	
87	- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
88	- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
89	- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
90	- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.
91	
92	## Environments
93	
94	- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
95	- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
96	- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
97	- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
98	- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.
99	
100	## Safety rules
101	
102	- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
103	- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
104	- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
105	- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
106	- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
107	- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
108	- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

253	/**
254	 * The families whose {@link GAME_PORT} entry is deliberately NOT the port a
255	 * player's own game client connects to — mapped to the port that actually is.
256	 *
257	 * `GAME_PORT` is a HEALTH-CHECK map. Where an image exposes a TCP port at all it
258	 * prefers that one, because "a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain connect,
259	 * and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up" — see its
260	 * own comment. For most families that port is also the join port, so the
261	 * distinction never mattered. For the eight below it is an RCON/query/admin
262	 * port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have always said so.
263	 *
264	 * It started mattering the moment provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's
265	 * own port" for NAT servers using this same map. Found live 2026-09-06 by
266	 * provisioning a real Rust server on node-2: the guest listened correctly on
267	 * 28015/udp (join) and 28016/tcp (RCON), the node's NAT had exactly one game
268	 * rule — 28016/tcp — and the dashboard handed the customer that RCON port as
269	 * their connect address. No player could ever have joined. That is the identical
270	 * outage found on the real paying customer `rust-w75hko` (see
271	 * docs/DOCUMENTATION.md's node migration section), whose root cause was
272	 * previously read as "allocateGameForward was never called for it"; it is called,
273	 * just with the wrong port.
274	 *
275	 * Every entry is sourced from the family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in
276	 * prisma/catalog.ts / the seed-wave*-games.ts files — the only ports docker
277	 * actually exposes off the container — cross-checked against the join port
278	 * `GAME_PORT`'s own comment already names. Anything NOT listed here joins on its
279	 * `GAME_PORT` entry; use {@link joinPortFor} rather than reading this directly.
280	 */
281	const GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE: Partial<Record<GameFamily, { port: number; protocol: "tcp" | "udp" }>> = {
282	  rust: { port: 28015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 28016/tcp rcon
283	  ark: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
284	  projectzomboid: { port: 16261, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
285	  factorio: { port: 34197, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
286	  arkasa: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
287	  // (soulmask needs no entry any more: its GAME_PORT is now 8777/udp — the port
288	  //  players join on — because its 18888/tcp admin port turned out to be bound
289	  //  to loopback inside the container and unreachable. See GAME_PORT.)
290	  squad: { port: 7787, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 21114/tcp rcon
291	  kf2: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 8080/tcp webadmin
292	  // Source-engine families: srcds binds the SAME port number on both protocols,
293	  // and the two are different services. UDP 27015 is the game + A2S query
294	  // protocol players and server browsers speak; TCP 27015 is RCON. Proven live
295	  // on a running Garry's Mod server 2026-09-07 — an A2S_INFO datagram to UDP
296	  // 27015 answered `ff ff ff ff 41 …` (S2C_CHALLENGE), while TCP 27015 accepted
297	  // the connection and returned nothing at all to the same query. Because the
298	  // port NUMBERS match, this one hid where the others didn't: the forward looked
299	  // right and was on the wrong protocol, so players could not connect AND the
300	  // single port left published to the internet was RCON — the exact exposure
301	  // `196e5c9` was written to end.
302	  gmod: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
303	  // 7 Days to Die is the same shape as the Source families above — it binds
304	  // 26900 on BOTH protocols and only the UDP one carries the game. Verified
305	  // live 2026-09-07: the server's own log says `[NET] Disabling protocol:
306	  // SteamNetworking` then `NET: LiteNetLib server started`, and LiteNetLib is
307	  // UDP-only; an A2S_INFO datagram to udp:26900 answered `ff ff ff ff 41 …`
308	  // (S2C_CHALLENGE) while tcp:26900 accepted the connection and replied with
309	  // four unrelated ASCII bytes. Matching port numbers hid this exactly the way
310	  // they hid it for Garry's Mod.
311	  sdtd: { port: 26900, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 26900/tcp
312	  tf2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
313	  l4d2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
314	  cs2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
315	  // (unturned needs no entry: its GAME_PORT is already 27015/udp — the same port
316	  //  players join on — because Unturned binds no TCP port at all. See GAME_PORT.)
317	};

483	 * These are FACTS ABOUT THE GAMES, not claims about Nxeon — Rust is a survival
484	 * game whoever is hosting it — which is why they can live in a static catalog
485	 * here rather than needing a column. They sit next to GAME_DISPLAY for the same
486	 * reason that map exists: the picker, the marketing pages and anything else that
487	 * wants to group games all read ONE list, instead of each growing its own copy
488	 * that drifts (the exact bug the GAME_DISPLAY comment above records).
489	 *
490	 * The vocabulary is deliberately CLOSED (the `Genre` union). An open-ended tag
491	 * string would let a typo — "Suvival" — silently become a seventh filter chip
492	 * showing one game, because the chip row is built from the genres actually
493	 * present rather than from a second hardcoded list.
494	 *
495	 * A family may be absent: it then answers only to "All games". Nothing here is
496	 * a popularity or sales signal — there is no honest one in the schema (every
497	 * active family carries a `featured` PLAN, which marks a tier inside a family,
498	 * not a favoured game), so the picker has no "Popular" chip.
499	 */
500	export type Genre = "Survival" | "Action" | "RPG" | "FPS" | "Strategy" | "Sandbox";
501	
502	/** Chip order in the picker. Only genres with at least one game are shown. */
503	export const GENRE_ORDER: Genre[] = ["Survival", "Action", "RPG", "FPS", "Strategy", "Sandbox"];

2913:model GamePlan {
2914-  id           String   @id @default(cuid())
2915-  gameFamily   String // minecraft, valheim, rust, palworld, cs2, terraria, ...
2916-  name         String // e.g. "Minecraft — 4 GB / 20 slots"
2917-  ramMB        Int
2918-  cpuCores     Int      @default(2)
2919-  diskGB       Int
2920-  slots        Int? // player slots (nullable)
2921-  priceCents   Int // retail price the customer pays (per term) — the REGULAR/renewal rate
2922-  /// GRANDFATHER PROGRAM (2026-09-17): mirrors Plan.introPriceCents/introTermMonths
2923-  /// exactly — a lower first-term price that renews at the regular `priceCents`
2924-  /// above. Read by the same generic lib/intro-pricing.ts helpers VPS already
2925-  /// uses (planIntroMonthlyCents/planIntroTermMonths take a `{priceCents}`-shaped
2926-  /// row, so a GamePlan works with zero new code there). NULL introTermMonths
2927-  /// means the WHOLE first term (any length) bills at introPriceCents.
2928-  introPriceCents Int?
2929-  introTermMonths Int?
2930-  termMonths   Int      @default(1)
2931-  basePlanId   String // the VPS Plan used to size/provision the VM
2932-  basePlan     Plan     @relation(fields: [basePlanId], references: [id])
2933-  osTemplateId String? // the game's OsTemplate (image) to deploy
2934-  featured     Boolean  @default(false)
2935-  active       Boolean  @default(true)
2936-  sortOrder    Int      @default(0)
2937-  createdAt    DateTime @default(now())
2938-  servers      Server[]
2939-}
2940-
2941-/// Mod-manager CATALOG: an installable mod/plugin for a game family. One row per
2942-/// mod per family; customers browse these and one-click install onto their server.
2943-/// Seeded from the per-game mod deep-dive research (name/category/source/id).
677:model OsTemplate {
678-  id              String        @id @default(cuid())
679-  slug            String        @unique
680-  name            String // display name, e.g. "Ubuntu"
681-  category        ImageCategory @default(PLAIN_OS)
682-  family          String        @default("linux") // ubuntu | debian | almalinux | rocky | cpanel | ...
683-  version         String        @default("") // "24.04", "13", ""
684-  logo            String        @default("") // icon slug for the UI
685-  vmid            Int // legacy/base template VMID to clone
686-  baseVmid        Int? // explicit base OS template for panels/apps (falls back to vmid)
687-  setupScript     String? // shell installed via cloud-init runcmd (panels/apps)
688-  minRamMB        Int           @default(1024)
689-  minDiskGB       Int           @default(10)
690-  licenseRequired Boolean       @default(false) // e.g. cPanel/Plesk need a paid license
691-  featured        Boolean       @default(false)
692-  sortOrder       Int           @default(0)
693-  active          Boolean       @default(true)
694-  servers         Server[]
695-}

I notice CS2 has two active plans both showing diskGB 100 rather than the expected 25-50 range. The worker provisioning logic falls back to the game plan's diskGB over the base plan's, so the VM ends up with 100GB even though the base Starter plan only specifies 25GB — which seems to contradict the assumption that a game plan should never exceed its base VPS tier.

I'm also spotting RAM mismatches: CS2's plan gives 2048MB but the CS2 OS template requires a 4096MB minimum, and similarly Rust's 4GB plan falls well under its template's 8192MB minimum despite Rust realistically needing 8-12GB for 40 slots — both look under-provisioned. Then there's Project Zomboid, where the 8GB/16-player tier actually has less disk (25GB) than the cheaper 6GB tier (30GB), which is an inverted pricing/disk relationship that would break any upgrade path since shrinking disk on resize isn't typically possible.

I'm now sanity-checking disk sizing across the rest of the game plans — ARK, ARK:SA, Squad, Satisfactory, 7 Days to Die, Conan, Empyrion — comparing each plan's disk allocation against realistic install sizes, and most seem reasonably sized so far.

Kill Floor 2 stands out as tight though: its install can run 14-15GB with all maps, which combined with OS and docker overhead against a 20GB plan feels risky, so I'm flagging that one for review as I continue checking Mordhau, Sandstorm, Space Engineers, and TF2.

These are rough estimates I'll flag as approximate. Now I need to check how RAM gets allocated to the VM — whether the worker provisioning uses the game plan's RAM value or falls back to the general plan's RAM, so I should grep for that logic.

21	 * GAME_CONFIG handler — apply a game server's customization (variant + settings).
22	 *
23	 * `worker/index.ts` owns the job loop and its `handlers` map; wire this in there:

27	 * this handler trusts `Server.gameVariant` / `Server.gameConfig`.
28	 *
29	 * TWO PATHS:
30	 *  - DEFAULT (simulation): records an "applied" marker on `Server.gameConfig` and
31	 *    notifies the user. No SSH, no VM mutation. This runs under SANDBOX and, in
32	 *    production, for any family not yet verified (see below).
33	 *
34	 *  - REAL: actually pushes the settings to the live game server over SSH. Runs
35	 *    per-family (see `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`) rather than one blanket switch — a
36	 *    family's real path is deliberately non-destructive (read-modify-write for
37	 *    key=value files, or — for images like Palworld's that regenerate their
38	 *    config from env vars on every boot — a full container recreation with
39	 *    rollback on failure; never clobbers a config it can't find/parse) and
40	 *    fully wrapped in try/catch so a failure notifies the user but never
41	 *    crashes the worker. `ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG=1` additionally force-enables
42	 *    every family at once, for whenever the rest have been confirmed too.
43	 *
44	 * Enable a family's real path only once its config paths / service names / apply
45	 * function have been confirmed for the actual game-server image — see
46	 * `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`'s own comment for what "confirmed" means in practice.

51	const REAL_APPLY_ENABLED = !SANDBOX && process.env.ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG === "1";

56	 * while `ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG` stays off for everyone else.
57	 *
58	 * "verified" here means: confirmed live, end-to-end, against a real running
59	 * container — not just "the code looks right". `palworld` was added
60	 * 2026-09-05 after the previous version of `applyPalworld` was found to
61	 * silently regenerate-then-lose its own writes (see that function's comment);
62	 * the replacement was verified by actually recreating a live container with
63	 * an updated setting and reading the resulting config back off disk.
64	 *
65	 * `minecraft` added 2026-09-06: verified against a real throwaway server on
66	 * node-2 (provisioned, applied `difficulty` + `online-mode` via
67	 * `applyRealConfig` directly, read `/opt/mc/server.properties` back off disk
68	 * and confirmed both values, then destroyed the VM). The path-detection
69	 * TODO on `applyMinecraft` is resolved for the current image: the host-side
70	 * bind mount (`/opt/mc` -> `/data`) puts server.properties somewhere
71	 * `remoteLocate`'s `find` over /opt already reaches. One real, non-blocking
72	 * gap found: `mcrcon` is not installed on the image, so today every setting
73	 * falls back to "restart to apply" — correctly reported as such, never
74	 * silently claimed live — rather than the live-RCON push `tryMinecraftRcon`
75	 * would otherwise attempt for difficulty/whitelist/etc.
76	 *
77	 * `rust` added 2026-09-06 by the whole-catalog integrity sweep, after
78	 * `applyRust` was found to be writing a `server.cfg` that (a) does not exist on
79	 * this image and (b) would have been ignored even if it did — see that
80	 * function's own comment for the two live proofs. The replacement recreates the
81	 * container from `RUST_SERVER_*` env vars, and was verified by reading **every
82	 * field in the Rust schema back off the live running game** via its own RCON,
83	 * not off a config file: `server.hostname: "NXEON SWEEP RUST"`,
84	 * `server.maxplayers: "42"`, `server.worldsize: "4000"`, `server.pve: "True"`,
85	 * and `server.seed: "12345"` still at its old value — proving untouched
86	 * settings survive the recreate. Independently corroborated by the server's own
87	 * boot log, whose occlusion grid went 1750 -> 2000 (worldsize/2) across the
88	 * change. One real caveat, reported to the customer in the apply's own notes
89	 * rather than hidden: Rust reloads its entire map on restart, so an apply takes
90	 * that server offline for several minutes — far longer than Palworld's seconds.
91	 *
92	 * `valheim` added 2026-09-06 by the same sweep. Its old implementation was the
93	 * worst-behaved of the three pre-written ones — it wrote a launch-args file
94	 * nothing read and returned `ok: true`, so the customer was told "Game settings

135	export async function gameConfigApply(job: Job): Promise<void> {
136	  const serverId = job.serverId;
137	  if (!serverId) throw new Error("game config: job has no serverId");
138	
139	  const server = await db.server.findUnique({
140	    where: { id: serverId },
141	    include: { osTemplate: true, gamePlan: true, dedicatedIp: true, node: true },
142	  });
143	  if (!server) throw new Error(`Server ${serverId} not found`);
144	
145	  const family = familyFor(server);
146	  const schema = schemaFor(family);
147	  if (!family || !schema) {
148	    throw new Error(`game config: ${server.hostname} is not a customizable game server`);
149	  }
150	
151	  const variant = server.gameVariant ?? schema.defaultVariant;
152	  const realApply = familyRealApplyEnabled(family);
153	
154	  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
155	  // Simulation is a SANDBOX affordance and MUST NEVER run in production.
156	  //
157	  // Until 2026-07-26 it did: production has no ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG, so every real
158	  // customer request fell through to the block below, stamped an `_appliedAt`
159	  // marker, and notified them "Game settings applied on <hostname>" — with the
160	  // "(sandbox)" suffix suppressed, because SANDBOX is false on production. So the
161	  // customer changed their difficulty or slot count, was told it was applied, and
162	  // nothing on the server had changed.
163	  //
164	  // Identical in kind to the SSL bug fixed the same day, where production wrote a
165	  // certificate row as ACTIVE with an invented expiry while no certbot had run:
166	  // the system asserting an outcome it never performed. A change we did not apply
167	  // is a FAILURE, and it must say so loudly enough that an operator notices the
168	  // flag is missing.
169	  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
170	  if (!realApply && !SANDBOX) {
171	    throw new Error(
172	      "Game settings could not be applied: real application is switched off on this " +
173	        "server (ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG is not set), so nothing was written to the game " +
174	        "server and your settings are NOT in effect. Please contact support."
175	    );
176	  }
177	
178	  if (!realApply) {
179	    const existing = (server.gameConfig as Record<string, unknown> | null) ?? {};
180	    const marker = {
181	      _appliedVariant: variant,
182	      _appliedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
183	      _configVersion: GAME_CONFIG_VERSION,
184	      _sandbox: SANDBOX,
185	    };
186	
187	    await db.server.update({
188	      where: { id: server.id },
189	      data: { gameConfig: { ...existing, ...marker } as any },
190	    });
191	
192	    await notify(
193	      server.userId,
194	      `Game settings applied on ${server.hostname}`,
195	      `${schema.label} (${variant}) settings were applied${SANDBOX ? " (sandbox)" : ""}.`,
196	      `/dashboard/servers/${server.id}?tab=game settings`
197	    );
198	    return;
199	  }
200	
201	  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
202	  // REAL PATH — gated behind ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG. Everything below is wrapped so
203	  // a failure notifies the user but never throws out of the handler.
204	  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
205	  const existing = (server.gameConfig as Record<string, unknown> | null) ?? {};
206	  const valid = validateConfig(family, existing);
207	  // `existing` also holds the `_`-prefixed markers; validateConfig drops unknown
208	  // keys, so `values` is exactly the schema fields keyed on the game's own keys.
209	  const values = valid.ok ? valid.values : {};
210	
211	  let outcome: ApplyOutcome = { ok: false, applied: [], notes: [] };
212	  try {
213	    outcome = await applyRealConfig(server, family, values);
214	  } catch (e) {
215	    const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);
216	    console.error(`[game-config] real apply failed on ${server.hostname}:`, e);
217	    outcome = { ok: false, applied: [], notes: [`Apply failed: ${msg}`] };
218	  }
219	
220	  // Always record the applied-marker (even on partial/soft failure) so the portal
221	  // reflects the attempt, and note whether the real push succeeded.
222	  const marker = {
223	    _appliedVariant: variant,
224	    _appliedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
225	    _configVersion: GAME_CONFIG_VERSION,
226	    _sandbox: SANDBOX,
227	    _real: true,
228	    _realOk: outcome.ok,
229	  };
230	  try {
231	    await db.server.update({
232	      where: { id: server.id },
233	      data: { gameConfig: { ...existing, ...marker } as any },
234	    });
235	  } catch (e) {
236	    console.error("[game-config] marker update failed", e);
237	  }
238	
239	  const detail = [...outcome.applied, ...outcome.notes].join(" ");
240	  await notify(
241	    server.userId,
242	    outcome.ok
243	      ? `Game settings applied on ${server.hostname}`
244	      : `Game settings partially applied on ${server.hostname}`,
245	    `${schema.label} (${variant}) — ${detail || "no changes were made."}`,
246	    `/dashboard/servers/${server.id}?tab=game settings`
247	  );
248	}

291	function buildCloudInit(server: any): string {
292	  const addons = (server.addons ?? {}) as {
293	    malwareScanner?: boolean;
294	    dailyBackup?: boolean;
295	    docker?: boolean;
296	    claudeCode?: boolean;
297	  };
298	  const setup: string[] = [];
299	
300	  // Pre-bake Claude Code (Anthropic CLI) on every server unless explicitly opted
301	  // out. Customers SSH in and run `claude` using their own subscription or API
302	  // key — no setup on our side, zero token cost to us. Installs run in the
303	  // background (nohup below) so the VM still reports ready quickly.
304	  if (addons.claudeCode !== false) {
305	    // Same steps the backfill (task #73) runs on existing servers — one source of
306	    // truth in lib/claude-install.ts, so cloud-init and backfill never drift.
307	    setup.push(...CLAUDE_CLI_INSTALL_STEPS);
308	  }
309	
310	  if (addons.docker) setup.push("curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh && systemctl enable --now docker");
311	  if (addons.malwareScanner)
312	    setup.push("(apt-get install -y clamav clamav-daemon || dnf install -y clamav) && (systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam || true)");
313	  if (server.osTemplate.setupScript) {
314	    // Translate the customer's checkout-time variant choice (Server.gameVariant)
315	    // into the actual install command BEFORE wrapping it into a systemd unit —
316	    // see applyGameVariant for why this substitution didn't exist until now.
317	    const scriptWithVariant = applyGameVariant(server.osTemplate.setupScript, server.osTemplate.family, server.gameVariant);
318	    // Same gap, generalized: the customer's checkout-time gameplay VALUES
319	    // (Server.gameConfig — e.g. DST's Klei cluster TOKEN, required for the
320	    // server to start at all) were captured and stored but never substituted
321	    // into the setupScript either, so the box always booted with the
322	    // template's static (usually blank) default. See applyGameConfigEnv.
323	    const scriptWithConfig = applyGameConfigEnv(
324	      scriptWithVariant,
325	      server.osTemplate.family,
326	      server.gameConfig as Record<string, unknown> | null,
327	    );
328	    // Minecraft's image tag is the ONE customization value that isn't a
329	    // `-e KEY=...` env var, so applyGameConfigEnv above never reaches it —
330	    // see applyMinecraftJavaImage's own comment for the live incident this
331	    // fixes (every Minecraft server provisioned on a hardcoded :java21
332	    // regardless of chosen VERSION). No-op for every other family.
333	    const scriptWithJavaImage = applyMinecraftJavaImage(
334	      scriptWithConfig,
335	      server.osTemplate.family,
336	      server.gameConfig as Record<string, unknown> | null,
337	    );
338	    // Per-server secrets a static catalog row can never hold for real (see
339	    // applyGameControlSecrets) — Palworld's ADMIN_PASSWORD doubles as the RCON
340	    // auth secret the player-list feature depends on, so every server needs
341	    // its own freshly generated value, never the catalog's shared placeholder.
342	    // Rust's RUST_RCON_PASSWORD is the same shape of gap, found 2026-09-10: the
343	    // placeholder didn't exist until this fix, so RCON (published on a public
344	    // port) fell back to the image's own well-known default password.
345	    const scriptWithSecrets =
346	      server.osTemplate.family === "palworld"
347	        ? applyGameControlSecrets(scriptWithJavaImage, { ADMIN_PASSWORD: generatePassword() })
348	        : server.osTemplate.family === "rust"
349	          ? applyGameControlSecrets(scriptWithJavaImage, { RUST_RCON_PASSWORD: generatePassword() })
350	          : server.osTemplate.family === "cs2"
351	            ? applyGameControlSecrets(scriptWithJavaImage, { CS2_RCONPW: generatePassword() })
352	            : scriptWithJavaImage;
353	    // Game images install as a bare `docker run -d` with no systemd unit, which

23	 * worker/index.ts) so it can be unit tested directly — importing
24	 * worker/index.ts runs its top-level `main()` job-polling loop.

26	import { schemaFor, minecraftImageForVersion } from "../lib/game-config";

28	export function applyGameVariant(setupScript: string, family: string | null, variant: string | null): string {
29	  if (family !== "minecraft") return setupScript;
30	  if (!variant) return setupScript;
31	  if (/-e\s+TYPE=/.test(setupScript)) return setupScript;
32	  const type = variant.toUpperCase();

53	 * `gameConfig` doesn't carry one (an order that never touched the field) —
54	 * matching today's catalog default (1.21.1 -> java21) exactly, so a customer
55	 * who never touches VERSION sees no change in behavior.
56	 */
57	export function applyMinecraftJavaImage(

95	 * escaping (`'\''`) so a customer-supplied string can never break out of the
96	 * quote and inject shell — the same safety property `validateConfig`'s own
97	 * control-character guard exists for, just extended to this second consumer
98	 * (a `docker run` command line) since the injection surface differs from a
99	 * line-oriented remote config file.

101	/**

103	 * setupScript, for a family whose image needs a real secret value that the
104	 * static catalog row can only ever leave blank — baking one directly into
105	 * the shared seed string (prisma/catalog.ts) would hand every future
106	 * customer the exact SAME value, since that row is one string shared by
107	 * every server of that family.

110	 * ticket: the platform's own player-list/RCON feature (lib/game-control.ts)
111	 * requires Palworld's ADMIN_PASSWORD to be set (it doubles as the RCON auth
112	 * secret) and RCON's port published, but the catalog's setupScript set
113	 * neither — so no Palworld server, ever provisioned, could support the
114	 * player-list feature customers are paying for. RCON_ENABLED/RCON_PORT are
115	 * not secrets, so those went directly into prisma/catalog.ts's setupScript
116	 * string; only this one per-server value needs runtime substitution.
117	 *
118	 * Same conservative shape as applyGameConfigEnv: only touches a key that's
119	 * already present as `-e KEY=...` in the script, and the caller decides what
120	 * counts as a "secret" for a given family — this function has no per-family
121	 * knowledge of its own.
122	 */
123	export function applyGameControlSecrets(
124	  setupScript: string,
125	  secrets: Record<string, string>,
126	): string {
127	  let out = setupScript;
128	  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(secrets)) {
129	    const re = new RegExp(`-e\\s+${key}=(?:'[^']*'|"[^"]*"|\\S*)`);
130	    if (!re.test(out)) continue;
131	    const escaped = value.replace(/'/g, `'\\''`);
132	    out = out.replace(re, `-e ${key}='${escaped}'`);
133	  }

138	  setupScript: string,

148	    if (raw === undefined || raw === null) continue;
149	    // envKey lets a readable schema key (e.g. "world") differ from the
150	    // literal docker env var name the image expects (e.g. "WORLD_NAME") —
151	    // see ConfigField.envKey's doc comment in lib/game-config.ts.
152	    const envName = field.envKey ?? field.key;
153	    const re = new RegExp(`-e\\s+${envName}=(?:'[^']*'|"[^"]*"|\\S*)`);
154	    if (!re.test(out)) continue; // this field isn't docker-env-driven in this script — leave it alone
155	    const escaped = String(raw).replace(/'/g, `'\\''`);
156	    out = out.replace(re, `-e ${envName}='${escaped}'`);
157	  }
158	  return out;

100	// Minecraft version -> required Java runtime (itzg/minecraft-server image tag)
101	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
102	
103	/**
104	 * Minimum Java major version each range of Minecraft releases genuinely
105	 * needs, per Mojang's own real cutovers (minecraft.wiki/w/Tutorials/
106	 * Update_Java, confirmed live 2026-09-20). Sorted newest-cutover-first; the
107	 * first entry whose `min` is <= the target version wins.
108	 *
109	 * FOUND LIVE 2026-09-20: `worker/game-config.ts`'s MINECRAFT_IMAGE was a
110	 * single hardcoded `itzg/minecraft-server:java21` for every Minecraft server
111	 * regardless of chosen VERSION, and `prisma/catalog.ts`'s provisioning
112	 * setupScript baked the identical literal tag in directly — only the
113	 * `VERSION` env var itself was ever substituted per-customer
114	 * (`applyGameConfigEnv`), never the image. 26.1 and newer (offered below in
115	 * MINECRAFT_RELEASE_VERSIONS) requires Java 25; Java 21 cannot run it at all.
116	 * Confirmed live via server minecraft-qj4rxt (customer picked 26.2): `docker
117	 * logs mc` -> "Minecraft 26.1 and newer requires running the server with Java
118	 * 25 or above.", container never actually started, every existing health
119	 * check (GAME_UPDATE/GAME_POWER) saw only "the container/service object
120	 * exists" and never noticed.
121	 *
122	 * Checked itzg/docker-minecraft-server's own docs (docs/versions/java.md) for
123	 * whether the image can auto-select the right JDK from the requested
124	 * VERSION — it explicitly cannot: tags are static per-Java-version, and the
125	 * docs point at this same Minecraft-wiki table for the mapping rather than
126	 * doing it themselves. `latest`/`stable` DO auto-track whichever Java the
127	 * newest release needs (java25 today) — but floating with whatever Mojang
128	 * ships next is exactly the footgun already fixed here once, for the VERSION
129	 * field itself (the 2026-09-06 Cobblemon incident — see MINECRAFT.fields'
130	 * VERSION comment below): an unannounced future Java bump on those tags
131	 * could just as easily break an old pinned-version modded server. A pinned,
132	 * versioned cutover table — maintained by hand the same deliberate way this
133	 * file already tracks MINECRAFT_RELEASE_VERSIONS — is the safer "plug and
134	 * play" shape: deterministic per Minecraft VERSION, one line to add when
135	 * Mojang's next real cutover ships.
136	 *
137	 * All five `javaN` tags below were verified to genuinely exist 2026-09-20
138	 * against Docker Hub's own registry API (HTTP 200 on each of java25/java21/
139	 * java17/java16/java8) — not assumed.
140	 */
141	const MINECRAFT_JAVA_CUTOVERS: { min: number[]; javaMajor: number }[] = [
142	  { min: [26, 1], javaMajor: 25 }, // 26.1 (26.1 Snapshot 1) and newer
143	  { min: [1, 20, 5], javaMajor: 21 }, // 1.20.5 (24w14a) – 1.21.11
144	  { min: [1, 18], javaMajor: 17 }, // 1.18 (Pre-release 2) – 1.20.4
145	  { min: [1, 17], javaMajor: 16 }, // 1.17 (21w19a) – 1.17.1
146	  { min: [0], javaMajor: 8 }, // everything older the platform still offers (down to 1.0)
147	];
148	
149	/** Parse a dotted numeric version string ("1.21.11", "26.2") into its components, or null (e.g. "LATEST"). */
150	function parseNumericVersion(v: string): number[] | null {
151	  if (!/^\d+(\.\d+)*$/.test(v)) return null;
152	  return v.split(".").map(Number);
153	}
154	
155	/** Compare two dotted-version component arrays, zero-padding the shorter one. */
156	function compareVersions(a: number[], b: number[]): number {
157	  const len = Math.max(a.length, b.length);
158	  for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
159	    const d = (a[i] ?? 0) - (b[i] ?? 0);
160	    if (d !== 0) return d;
161	  }
162	  return 0;
163	}
164	
165	/**
166	 * The minimum Java major version a given Minecraft VERSION genuinely
167	 * requires. "LATEST" (itzg's always-track-Mojang's-newest sentinel) can
168	 * resolve to any future release at boot, so it gets the same ceiling
169	 * `latest`/`stable` track today (Java 25) — the highest requirement of
170	 * anything currently offered. A newer JVM running an older Minecraft server
171	 * is the one direction that's genuinely safe (matching or exceeding the real
172	 * requirement, never falling short of it), so an unrecognized/future version
173	 * string also fails safe to this same ceiling rather than guessing low.
174	 */
175	export function requiredJavaMajorForMinecraftVersion(version: string): number {
176	  if (version === "LATEST") return 25;
177	  const parsed = parseNumericVersion(version);
178	  if (!parsed) return 25;
179	  for (const cutover of MINECRAFT_JAVA_CUTOVERS) {
180	    if (compareVersions(parsed, cutover.min) >= 0) return cutover.javaMajor;
181	  }
182	  return 8;
183	}
184	
185	/** The itzg/minecraft-server image tag that satisfies a given Minecraft VERSION's real Java requirement. */
186	export function minecraftImageForVersion(version: string): string {
187	  return `itzg/minecraft-server:java${requiredJavaMajorForMinecraftVersion(version)}`;
188	}
189	
190	/**
191	 * The Java major version an itzg/minecraft-server image reference is tagged
192	 * for, or null when it can't be determined (a bare/untagged image, or
193	 * anything not matching the `:javaN` convention) — treated as "unknown,"
194	 * never assumed sufficient.
195	 */
196	export function javaMajorOfMinecraftImage(image: string | null | undefined): number | null {
197	  if (!image) return null;
198	  const m = /:java(\d+)\b/.exec(image);
199	  return m ? Number(m[1]) : null;
200	}

content.thinking:
This is a major finding: for 37 non-real-apply families, the only way a checkout setting actually takes effect is through the `-e KEY=` environment variables in setupScript, and many of these families have zero wired fields at all—satisfactory, sdtd, vrising, factorio, gmod, conan, unturned, and a long list of others.

Aceengineers is a stark example: every checkout setting is captured but never applied. content.thinking:
I'm realizing variant handling is inconsistent across families — for non-Minecraft games, variants only get applied through the game-specific config path, so an ARK customer picking "Ragnarok" would actually end up with The Island, and PZ's "b41" selection silently becomes b42 since the branch field stays blank. VRising has its own pvp/pve/duo variants to account for too.

Counting up all the games with variant options — ark, satisfactory, projectzomboid, vrising, factorio, gmod, conan, unturned, theforest, sonsoftheforest, cs2, icarus, arkasa, soulmask, dst, vintagestory, tf2, l4d2 — that's a lot of surface area where the wizard might be showing choices that don't actually get respected server-side. The ARK Ragnarok-becomes-Island case stands out as the clearest example of selling a customization option that's silently ignored.

I'm also wondering about the blank admin password default — when that gets wired through, it overrides the catalog's default password with an empty string, which seems like a real security concern for something like PZ.

Since validateConfig fills in every missing field, orders always end up with a fully-populated config. So for families where password fields go unfilled by the user, they end up passing through as blank rather than falling back to something safe. For families where the field is never wired into the setup script at all, the catalog's static default value just stays untouched.

This looks like a real widespread issue: ARK Survival Ascended's admin password key isn't wired at all, so `changeme12` persists on every single ASA server — meaning any player could enable cheats and become admin. Same pattern seems to affect The Forest, Sons of the Forest, and potentially L4D2's RCON password depending on how blank values are handled by srcds.

Then I check Killing Floor 2, TF2, Mordhau, Dragonwilds, and Icarus similarly — KF2's admin password defaults to blank with WebAdmin enabled on an exposed port, which could allow unauthenticated login, though I flag this as needing verification. Mordhau and Dragonwilds properly require their admin passwords to be set, while Icarus also defaults to a blank admin password.

The real finding I want to nail down: Arkasa hard-codes its admin password to "changeme12" on every server because there's a key mismatch — the schema expects `AdminPassword` but the env var is `SERVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, so the customer's chosen password is never actually applied. I want to verify this by checking the Arkasa schema lines around 1533-1551.

/**
 * Game server control panel — SSH/RCON transport + per-family control facts.
 *
 * A plain server-side module (NO "use server", no client imports). Imported by
 * BOTH the server actions (lib/actions-game-control.ts) and the worker
 * (worker/game-control.ts). It NEVER runs in the browser — the customer's root
 * credentials and their server's RCON password stay on our server.
 *
 * Everything here operates on the CUSTOMER'S OWN game VM over the platform's
 * existing SSH (host/port/root-password derived exactly like lib/sftp.ts, reused
 * via lib/ssh-exec.ts `withServerSsh`). Two transport rules, mirroring the rest of
 * the control panel:
 *
 *   1. STRICT ALLOWLIST VALIDATION for anything that reaches a shell. Ports, unit
 *      names, paths and file names are validated/allowlisted or rejected — never
 *      sanitized. Family/unit hints are compile-time constants, never customer
 *      input.
 *
 *   2. RCON never touches a shell at all. We read the server's RCON port/password
 *      out of its own config file, then open a TCP channel to 127.0.0.1:<port> on
 *      the game VM THROUGH the SSH connection (`conn.forwardOut`) and speak the
 *      Source RCON wire protocol directly. The RCON port is never exposed off the
 *      box, the password is only ever a protocol packet body (not an argv token),
 *      and the customer's console command is validated to be single-line/control-
 *      char-free before it is sent.
 *
 * SANDBOX: callers gate real SSH behind `!SANDBOX`; on staging the inline reads
 * return realistic synthetic data so the whole UX works without a live VM.
 */

import { GAME_FAMILIES, type GameFamily } from "./games";

/**
 * Game auto-update: the remote script, its output parser, and the verdict.
 *
 * INCIDENT ("Game auto-update cannot fail", honest inventory #3): the old
 * `updateCommand` returned
 *
 *     set -e; <steam>; <restart>; true
 *
 * where the steamcmd call ended `|| true` and was skipped entirely when steamcmd
 * was absent, every restart branch ended `|| true`, and the whole command ended
 * `; true`. The remote command could NOT exit non-zero. So `gameUpdate` always
 * reached its notification and always told the customer *"The latest server
 * update was applied and the service was restarted."* — for a box where steamcmd
 * was not installed, where no matching systemd unit existed, or where the service
 * came back dead. This runs unattended every 6 hours.
 *
 * `worker/apps.ts` is the model this follows: every operation declares what it
 * PROVES, the remote side emits explicit markers, and an exit code of 0 is never
 * accepted as evidence. (`wp_die()` prints its error and exits 0 — that is the
 * lesson, and `|| true` is the same lesson wearing a different hat.)
 *
 * A second honesty problem is fixed here too: minecraft and terraria have no
 * steamcmd app id, so for those families the job never updated ANYTHING — it
 * restarted a service. The success message now says which of the two happened.
 *
 * Pure and dependency-free: no SSH, no clock. Covered by test/game-update.test.ts,
 * which also runs `sh -n` and `dash -n` over the generated script.
 */

/**
 * Steam dedicated-server app IDs for families whose game files are updated by
 * steamcmd running DIRECTLY ON THE HOST, next to a systemd unit that manages the
 * server process itself (not a container).
 *
 * valheim/rust/palworld/cs2 were REMOVED from this table 2026-09-10, found live
 * via a real customer's Valheim server (`terraheim`) failing its GAME_UPDATE job
 * on every single run for 2 days straight with "steamcmd is not installed" —
 * true, but not fixable, because all four are actually Docker-run
 * (`OsTemplate.setupScript` installs Docker and `docker run`s an image; a thin
 * systemd unit wraps it as `ExecStart=docker start -a <name>` purely so the rest
 * of the platform can treat it like any other service). steamcmd for these lives
 * inside the container's own image, if it exists at all — never on the host —
 * so `command -v steamcmd` on the host can never succeed, and the job was
 * pointlessly retrying and re-notifying the customer every ~6h/24h forever for
 * 5 real live servers (3 valheim, 1 rust, 1 palworld) with zero chance of ever
 * resolving. This is the exact bug class already fixed for waves 3/4/8/9 and
 * the Plutonium family below — those all correctly stayed OUT of this table
 * from the start; these four just predate that convention and were never
 * migrated onto it until now. Restart-only (via the wrapper unit, confirmed
 * live to correctly call `docker start -a`/`docker stop`) is what these get
 * instead — see `updatesFromSteam()`.
 */
export const STEAM_APPID: Partial<Record<GameFamily, string>> = {};

/** systemd service name candidates per family (first that exists wins). */
export const SERVICE_HINT: Record<GameFamily, string> = {
  minecraft: "minecraft",
  valheim: "valheim",

131	/** Does this family have an update source at all, or is the job only a restart? */
132	export function updatesFromSteam(family: GameFamily): boolean {
133	  return Boolean(STEAM_APPID[family]);
134	}
135	
136	/** Seconds we wait for the unit to come back before we stop claiming anything. */
137	export const RESTART_WAIT_TRIES = 30;
138	export const RESTART_WAIT_SLEEP_S = 2;
139	
140	/**
141	 * Should `gameUpdateSweep` even enqueue a check for this candidate?
142	 *
143	 * `Server.status` is the VM's own power state, not the game service inside
144	 * it — `gamePower`'s own doc comment (worker/game-control.ts) is explicit
145	 * that the two are "genuinely different things". So a customer who presses
146	 * Stop on the dashboard (GAME_POWER "stop") leaves `status` at RUNNING
147	 * forever, and the sweep — which only ever looks at `status`+`autoUpdate` —
148	 * kept enqueueing a GAME_UPDATE job against it every cycle with no way to
149	 * know the service was off on purpose. Every one of those jobs then failed
150	 * with "your game server is NOT running", which is TRUE and also not news:
151	 * the customer did that themselves.
152	 *
153	 * Found live 2026-09-17: suplosmp (bedrock) generated a FAILED GAME_UPDATE
154	 * job on every single sweep for 28+ straight hours after its owner pressed
155	 * Stop and hadn't turned it back on — the same "customer would learn to
156	 * ignore it" erosion `notifyFailureOnce` already exists to prevent for
157	 * notifications, just unaddressed on the job-creation side.
158	 *
159	 * `gamePower` persists the post-action `systemctl is-active` result to
160	 * `Server.gameConfig._serviceState` (its own doc comment explains why: the
161	 * dashboard's status dot needed it). That is the one signal that distinguishes
162	 * "the customer turned this off" from "this crashed" — a crash is never
163	 * written here, only an explicit start/stop/restart action is. So only the
164	 * exact value "inactive" (a clean, completed stop) skips the sweep; anything
165	 * else — "failed" (a crash), "activating" (mid-restart), missing/stale — is
166	 * still checked normally, because those are precisely what this job exists
167	 * to catch.
168	 */
169	export function eligibleForUpdateSweep(gameConfig: unknown): boolean {
170	  const state = (gameConfig as Record<string, unknown> | null | undefined)?.["_serviceState"];
171	  return state !== "inactive";
172	}
173	
174	/**
175	 * Build the remote script.
176	 *
177	 * Design rules, each of which the old one-liner broke:
178	 *
179	 *  - No `set -e` and no trailing `; true`. Control flow is explicit, and the exit
180	 *    status is irrelevant — the MARKERS are the contract, so a truncated or
181	 *    dropped connection is detectable (no `NXGU:END`) rather than indistinguishable
182	 *    from success.
183	 *  - steamcmd's own exit code is not trusted (it is famously unreliable and
184	 *    frequently non-zero on a perfectly good update). We match its own success
185	 *    line instead, and report the code alongside.
186	 *  - "no unit matched" is an outcome we emit, not a branch we swallow.
187	 *  - The post-restart state is polled and reported verbatim. `active` is the only
188	 *    thing that will be called success upstream.
189	 *
190	 * `family` is constrained to GAME_FAMILIES by the caller AND re-checked here, so
191	 * nothing unvalidated is interpolated into the shell.
192	 */
193	export function updateCommand(family: GameFamily): string {
194	  if (!GAME_FAMILIES.includes(family)) throw new Error(`not a game family: ${family}`);
195	  const appId = STEAM_APPID[family];
196	  const svc = SERVICE_HINT[family];
197	  // Both are compile-time constants from the tables above — never customer input.
198	
199	  // Emitted by every branch that must not go on to restart the service.
200	  const stopHere = [
201	    `st=$(systemctl is-active "$unit" 2>/dev/null)`,
202	    `say "SKIPPED_RESTART:1"`,
203	    `say "STATE:${"$"}{st:-unknown}"`,
204	    `say "END"`,
205	    `exit 0`,
206	  ];
207	
208	  const steam = appId
209	    ? [
210	        `fresh=0`,
211	        `if command -v steamcmd >/dev/null 2>&1; then`,
212	        `  out=$(steamcmd +login anonymous +app_update ${appId} validate +quit 2>&1); rc=$?`,
213	        `  say "STEAM_RC:$rc"`,
214	        // steamcmd prints "Success! App '<id>' already up to date." when there was
215	        // nothing to download, and "Success! App '<id>' fully installed." when
216	        // there was. Both used to match one grep, so the two outcomes were
217	        // indistinguishable — see the CURRENT/OK split in the header note.
218	        `  if printf '%s' "$out" | grep -q "Success! App '${appId}' already up to date"; then`,
219	        `    say "STEAM:CURRENT"`,
220	        `  elif printf '%s' "$out" | grep -q "Success! App '${appId}'"; then`,
221	        `    fresh=1; say "STEAM:OK"`,
222	        `  else`,
223	        `    say "STEAM:FAIL"`,
224	        `    printf '%s' "$out" | grep -i 'error' | head -3 | while IFS= read -r l; do say "STEAM_ERR:$l"; done`,
225	        `  fi`,
226	        `else`,
227	        `  say "STEAM:ABSENT"`,
228	        `fi`,
229	        // Do NOT bounce a healthy game server for an update that did not happen:
230	        // a restart kicks every connected player off for nothing, and it would
231	        // make "the service was restarted" the only true half of a false claim.
232	        // This now also covers the "already up to date" case, which is the COMMON
233	        // one — it ran every 6 hours and disconnected everybody four times a day.
234	        `if [ "$fresh" != "1" ]; then`,
235	        ...stopHere.map((l) => `  ${l}`),
236	        `fi`,
237	      ].join("\n")
238	    : [
239	        // No update source exists for this family, so there is nothing a restart
240	        // could apply. Restarting anyway is a pure loss: every connected player
241	        // is disconnected, four times a day, forever, to change nothing. The
242	        // rule two paragraphs up applies here MOST, and used not to be applied
243	        // here at all.
244	        `say "STEAM:NA"`,
245	        ...stopHere,
246	      ].join("\n");
247	
248	  return [
249	    `say() { printf 'NXGU:%s\\n' "$1"; }`,
250	    // 1. Resolve the unit. `systemctl cat` succeeds only for a unit that exists.
251	    `unit=""`,
252	    `for c in ${svc} ${svc}-server; do`,
253	    `  if systemctl cat "$c" >/dev/null 2>&1; then unit="$c"; break; fi`,
254	    `done`,
255	    `if [ -z "$unit" ]; then`,
256	    `  unit=$(systemctl list-units --type=service --plain --no-legend 2>/dev/null | grep -i ${family} | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')`,
257	    `fi`,
258	    `if [ -z "$unit" ]; then say "UNIT:NONE"; say "END"; exit 0; fi`,
259	    `say "UNIT:$unit"`,
260	    `was=$(systemctl is-active "$unit" 2>/dev/null); say "WAS:${"$"}{was:-unknown}"`,
261	    // 2. Update the game files, where such a thing exists.
262	    steam,
263	    // 3. Restart, and report the real result of the restart call.
264	    `systemctl restart "$unit" >/dev/null 2>&1; say "RESTART_RC:$?"`,
265	    // 4. Wait for it to settle. A game server can take a while to open its port,
266	    //    so "activating" is a distinct answer from "failed" and both are reported.
267	    `i=0; st=""`,
268	    `while [ $i -lt ${RESTART_WAIT_TRIES} ]; do`,
269	    `  st=$(systemctl is-active "$unit" 2>/dev/null)`,
270	    `  if [ "$st" = "active" ] || [ "$st" = "failed" ]; then break; fi`,
271	    `  i=$((i+1)); sleep ${RESTART_WAIT_SLEEP_S}`,
272	    `done`,
273	    `say "STATE:${"$"}{st:-unknown}"`,
274	    `say "END"`,
275	  ].join("\n");
276	}
277	
278	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
279	// Parsing
280	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
281	
282	export type GameUpdateFacts = {
283	  /** The systemd unit the script acted on, or null when nothing matched. */
284	  unit: string | null;
285	  /** `systemctl is-active` before the restart. */
286	  wasActive: string;
287	  /** Exit code of `systemctl restart`, or null when it never ran. */

### Stationeers cannot be sold today — the image drives a build it no longer matches

Installs cleanly (13.3 GB into a writable mount, healthy container, no restart loop)
but the game **never binds any port, TCP or UDP**, and never creates a world —
`saves/` stayed empty after 10+ minutes across three configurations.

`didstopia/stationeers-server`'s `start.sh` always appends `-worldname=X -loadworld=X`
unquoted from image ENV defaults (`STATIONEERS_WORLD_NAME=docker`), and tests them with
`${VAR+x}` (set-or-not), so passing an empty value does not suppress them. Along the
way: the catalog set `STATIONEERS_WORLD_NAME='Nxeon World'` — a value **with a space** —
which the unquoted interpolation split into `-worldname=Nxeon World -loadworld=Nxeon
World`. Fixing that was necessary and still not sufficient; supplying modern
`-settings StartLocalHost true …` still had the legacy flags appended after it and the
container exited 127.

**This needs the owner**, exactly like CS2's and Conan's: replacing the image (or
writing a full entrypoint override, as was done for Eco above) is a catalog decision,
not a setup-script tweak, and was not guessed at here.

content.content:
`itzg/minecraft-server` image with no `-e VERSION=...`. That image defaults `VERSION=LATEST`
and re-resolves it against Mojang's manifest **on every container restart**, upgrading the
installed server jar in place — exactly the kind of drift `lib/free-minecraft-control.ts`'s
`FREEMC_PLUGIN_MC_VERSION` pin already existed to prevent, just never ported from the free
tier to the paid game-hosting catalog.

Fix, in two commits after live verification caught a second bug the first one missed:
1. Pinned `VERSION='1.21.1'` in the catalog setup script, added a real "Minecraft version"
   field (`lib/game-config.ts`, key `VERSION`) so customers can choose/change it in Settings
   instead of it being invisible, and wired `worker/game-config.ts`'s `applyMinecraft` to
   recreate the `mc` container (env-file-driven, converting away from the old inline `-e`
   flags) only when the pinned version actually changes.
2. **Verifying that fix live** (`docker inspect` + `docker run --entrypoint sh ... java
   -version` against the real customer VM, not assumed) found the bare `itzg/minecraft-server`
   image bundles ONE FIXED JRE per tag — it does NOT auto-select a JRE per the requested
   `VERSION` the way itzg's docs read on a first pass. The container's `VERSION` pinned
   correctly to 1.21.1 but it kept running the image's bundled JDK 25. Fixed by pinning the
   image to `itzg/minecraft-server:java21` (confirmed live: Temurin 21.0.12 LTS) in both the
   catalog script and `worker/game-config.ts`'s `MINECRAFT_IMAGE`, and extending the same
   settings-apply guard to also recreate the container when its running image doesn't match
   the current tag — so any server provisioned before this fix self-heals the next time its
   settings are saved, not just newly provisioned ones.

Residual, NOT a platform bug: after both fixes, the reporting customer's own container still
would not boot — their installed mod set is missing three dependency mods entirely (`tim_core`,
`rctapi`, `sophisticatedcore`) and separately includes `c2me-opts-natives-math`, a performance
mod that itself demands Java 25+ — directly conflicting with the Java 21 that 1.21.1 and their
other mods need. That is an incompatible/incomplete mod list on the customer's own side, found
via the container's real crash log, not something the platform silently auto-installs a guess
for.

If a future customer pins a MUCH older or newer `VERSION` than 1.21.1 via the Settings field,
today's fixed `:java21` image tag can itself become this exact bug again — there is no
per-version Java tag lookup yet. Revisit if that gap is ever hit for real, rather than building
it speculatively now.

**Verified live on the same VM** by applying exactly what the fixed script does — stop the unit,
`chown -R 7100:7100 /opt/conan`, recreate the container — and watching the behaviour invert:
`wine: created the configuration directory '/conanexiles/.wine'` (was "refusing to create"),
`Success! App '443030' fully installed.`, `/opt/conan/game` **6.2 GB** (was 4.0K), the config symlink
`ConanSandbox/nxeon -> /conanexiles_config` created without error, and `NRestarts=0` (was 38).

### Blocker 2 — the server binary itself never starts (OWNER DECISION, not fixed)

With the mount bug fixed and the game fully installed *into the mount*, `ConanSandboxServer.exe`
launches under Wine and then does nothing at all. Across two full boots and 35+ minutes:

- the process is alive (`Z:\conanexiles\ConanSandboxServer.exe --userdir=nxeon ... -server -log`)
- it has burned **7 CPU ticks total** — `utime stime` = `2 5`, unchanged over a 45-second sample
- it holds 459 MB and 0.00% CPU, on a box with 5.2 GB free and no OOM kills
- `/proc/net/udp` and `/proc/net/tcp` inside the container are **empty** — nothing bound
- nothing is ever written to `/conanexiles_config` (`Saved/Logs/ConanSandbox.log` never appears —
  the image's own `tail` of it fails forever), and `find` turns up no game log anywhere on the box

A second boot, which skips the download entirely, behaves identically. So the mount fix is necessary
and correct — it is a strict improvement, and the customer's install and saves now live in the
persistent mount instead of a disposable container layer — but it is **not sufficient**:
`melle2/conanexiles-ds:latest` does not produce a working Conan Exiles server on this platform.

**This needs the owner**, exactly like CS2's: Conan Exiles is on sale at $14.99/$24.99/$39.99 and
cannot currently be delivered at any tier. Resolving it means sourcing and validating a different
dedicated-server image (or a native, non-Wine install path), which is a catalog/product decision with
real research behind it — not a bug fix. Until then every Conan order will fail provisioning after
~30 minutes of trying.

content.content:
## CS2 cannot be provisioned at all, on any plan — three blockers (2026-09-06, OWNER DECISION)

The catalog sweep's first outright provisioning failure, and unlike everything else found that day
it is **not** a bug to fix in code — it needs a product call. Recorded here so nobody re-diagnoses it.

A CS2 order fails 100% of the time. Three independent causes, each confirmed on a real VM:

**1. Every CS2 plan's disk is far too small.** SteamCMD's own words, from the container's
`content_log.txt`:

```
AppID 730 update canceled : Failed to preallocate (Not enough disk space) "58.42 GB"
AppID 730 scheduler finished : removed from schedule (result Not enough disk space, state 0x202)
```

and the full download is **71,089,554,542 bytes — 66.2 GiB**. CS2's two plans are Starter (25GB,
$6.99) and Standard (50GB, $11.99); their own `gamePlan.diskGB` values are 40GB and 50GB. None of
those can hold it. A retest on an 80GB Pro-sized VM got the download running — proving nothing else
about the image is fundamentally broken — but it was down to **25GB free at 65.6%**, with ~24GB of
download plus the whole install/extract step still to come. That retest was stopped there rather
than run to its conclusion, so treat "80GB also fails" as a strong projection from those numbers,
not an observed failure; what IS observed is that 25/40/50GB fail outright and 80GB leaves no
headroom. **Assume the 120GB tier or a CS2-specific one is required.** That changes CS2's cost basis
and therefore its price, which is why this stops here rather than being "fixed".

**2. The bind mount is unusable, so the data would not survive anyway.** `/opt/cs2` is created
`root:root 0755` and the `joedwards32/cs2` container runs as `uid=1000(steam)` — hence
`Failed to create "/home/steam/cs2-dedicated/steamapps" folder` in its log. Verified on the 80GB
retest: at 63% downloaded, `/opt/cs2` was still 4.0K and every byte was landing in the **container's
own writable layer**. Any `docker rm`/recreate — including the settings-apply path this sweep just
built for other families — would delete the customer's entire server. CS2 is the only family checked
so far whose image neither runs as root nor honours `PUID`/`PGID` (satisfactory, projectzomboid,
sdtd and enshrouded all set those; rust, valheim, minecraft and palworld run as root or chown for
themselves). The fix, whenever the disk decision lands, is `mkdir -p /opt/cs2 && chown 1000:1000
/opt/cs2` ahead of the `docker run` in its `setupScript` — in `prisma/catalog.ts` **and** the live
`OsTemplate.setupScript` row.

**3. The game-port health check cannot cover a ~70GB install.** `GAME_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` is
300s, and three job attempts still only buys ~15 minutes. The 80GB retest was barely half
downloaded when the job hit `FAILED` on attempt 3. Any family whose image install runs longer than
that will fail provisioning regardless of health — worth a per-family timeout (or one derived from
image size) rather than a single global constant.

### Related: 116 of 121 game plans just got smaller disks

Independently, `c59d9bc` (a concurrent session, same morning) changed `provision()` to size game VMs
from `gamePlan` — the advertised numbers — instead of the linked `basePlan`. That is the right
principle, but measured against the live catalog **116 of 121 game plans shrink**, several sharply
(Abiotic Factor 6GB: 80→25GB; ARK 8GB: 80→40GB; Bedrock 1GB: 25→5GB; Conan 6GB: 80→30GB). CS2 is
unaffected in outcome — it was impossible at either size — but it raises the same question for every
other family: **is each advertised disk actually big enough for that game's install?** Nobody has
checked, and the biggest installs (arkasa, ark, sdtd, conan, icarus) are where it would bite first.

`lib/games.ts`'s `GAME_PORT` comment has said this since the check was written: it exists because
"a Terraria order silently sat on an interactive world-selection prompt with no TTY — the container
showed 'Up' while nothing ever bound the port, and PROVISION reported success anyway". The check was
added, and has been correctly catching it ever since. **The underlying cause was never fixed**, so
the outcome simply changed from "reports success, server is dead" to "every Terraria order fails" —
which is where the catalog sweep found it, reproduced exactly, on the first try.
