196	 * Intentionally conservative: any setupScript that doesn't match the exact
197	 * `docker run -d --name X ...` shape (or any non-game family, e.g. the
198	 * LAMP/WordPress/Caddy panel images that already install a real native systemd
199	 * service) is returned completely unchanged.
200	 */
201	function wrapDockerGameService(setupScript: string, family: string | null): string {
202	  if (!isGameFamily(family)) return setupScript;
203	  const unitName = controlSpec(family)?.serviceHints[0];
204	  if (!unitName) return setupScript;
205	
206	  const re = /docker run\s+(?:-d|--detach)\b(.*?)\s+--name[= ]("?)([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\2(.*)$/.exec(setupScript.trim());
207	  if (!re) return setupScript;
208	  const [full, before, , containerName, after] = re;
209	  const matchIndex = setupScript.indexOf(full);
210	  if (matchIndex < 0) return setupScript;
211	
212	  // Strip docker's own restart policy — systemd now owns restart semantics for
213	  // this container, and leaving both in place makes the two supervisors fight
214	  // over a crash-looping process.
215	  const cleanedAfter = after.replace(/\s*--restart(?:=|\s+)\S+/, "");
216	  // Cap the container's json-file log driver. No game image's setupScript ever
217	  // set this, so a crash-looping container (systemd restarting it every 5s
218	  // forever — see RestartSec above) grows an unbounded log file. Root-caused
219	  // live 2026-09-17 on projectzomboid-kc0kcr: its docker json log alone had
220	  // grown to ~28 GB (on top of ~28.5 GB of rsyslog spamming its own
221	  // "no space left on device" write failures once the disk filled), filling
222	  // the 77 GB root disk to 100% and taking the game server down. This is the
223	  // single construction point every game family's `docker run` is rewritten
224	  // through, so applying the cap here covers all of them at once rather than
225	  // editing each family's setupScript individually. 10m x 3 files = a 30 MB
226	  // ceiling per container regardless of how long or how hard it crash-loops.
227	  const createCmd = `docker create --name ${containerName} --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3${before}${cleanedAfter}`
228	    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
229	    .trim();
230	
231	  const prefix = setupScript.slice(0, matchIndex);
232	  const unit = [
233	    `cat > /etc/systemd/system/${unitName}.service <<'NXUNIT'`,
234	    "[Unit]",
235	    `Description=Nxeon game service (docker: ${containerName})`,
236	    "After=docker.service",
237	    "Requires=docker.service",
238	    "",
239	    "[Service]",
240	    `ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker start -a ${containerName}`,
241	    `ExecStop=/usr/bin/docker stop -t 30 ${containerName}`,
242	    "Restart=always",
243	    "RestartSec=5",
244	    "TimeoutStartSec=0",
245	    "",
246	    "[Install]",
247	    "WantedBy=multi-user.target",
248	    "NXUNIT",
249	    "systemctl daemon-reload",
250	    `systemctl enable --now ${unitName}`,
251	  ].join("\n");
252	
253	  return `${prefix}${createCmd}\n${unit}`;
254	}

262	 * The nxeon-shipper install: fetch the static binary, drop its config (server
263	 * id + per-server token minted by the caller, see provision()), install the
264	 * systemd unit, and start it. Idempotent (safe to re-run on a retried
265	 * provision) and — like the Claude CLI install — backgrounded via the outer
266	 * nohup so a slow/blocked download never delays the VM reporting ready.
267	 *
268	 * `curl -fsSL … | sh`-style external installs are the established convention
269	 * here (see get.docker.com / claude.ai/install.sh above); this one pulls from
270	 * our own APP_URL instead of a third party since the binary is ours.
271	 */
272	function shipperInstallScript(serverId: string, token: string, nodeKind: "VPS" | "GAME"): string {
273	  const appUrl = process.env.APP_URL ?? "https://nxeon.cloud";
274	  const config = JSON.stringify({
275	    server_id: serverId,
276	    token,
277	    ingest_url: `${appUrl}/api/telemetry/ingest`,
278	    node_kind: nodeKind,
279	  });
280	  return [
281	    "mkdir -p /etc/nxeon",
282	    `cat > /etc/nxeon/shipper.json <<'NXTJSON'\n${config}\nNXTJSON`,
283	    "chmod 600 /etc/nxeon/shipper.json",
284	    `curl -fsSL "${appUrl}/dl/nxeon-shipper-linux-amd64" -o /usr/local/bin/nxeon-shipper.tmp && ` +
285	      "chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nxeon-shipper.tmp && mv /usr/local/bin/nxeon-shipper.tmp /usr/local/bin/nxeon-shipper",
286	    `curl -fsSL "${appUrl}/dl/nxeon-shipper.service" -o /etc/systemd/system/nxeon-shipper.service`,
287	    "systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now nxeon-shipper",
288	  ].join("\n");
289	}

content.thinking:
I'm working out Satisfactory's networking ports—base game uses 7777 for TCP/UDP, and the 1.1 update apparently added port 8888 TCP for reliable messaging, so I need to confirm which ports are actually required now.

Actually, this reveals a real problem: Satisfactory's game traffic runs on UDP 7777, while the TCP 7777 is only the HTTPS server-manager API. So a NAT setup forwarding just 7777/tcp would let admins claim the server but players couldn't actually join, since UDP never gets forwarded—a high severity issue, though moot given Satisfactory has no live servers. Conan Exiles has the same mismatch (game traffic on UDP 7777/7778 plus a 27015 UDP query port, versus only TCP 7777 forwarded), though again moot since Conan never starts. I'm now checking The Isle's Evrima build, which I believe uses UDP 7777 for gameplay and TCP 10000 for its queue system, meaning a TCP-only forward could leave it similarly unjoinable.

Stationeers likely needs UDP 27500 despite only TCP being forwarded, but that's moot since it's broken anyway. Terraria and Minecraft look correctly configured with TCP. For 7 Days to Die, I'm weighing whether the unforwarded 26901/26902 UDP ports actually matter given LiteNetLib appears to run solely on 26900 with Steam networking disabled. For ARK: Survival Evolved, I'm considering whether the missing 27015 UDP query port only affects Steam server browser visibility rather than direct IP connections, since `open ip:port` connects without needing the query port.

Now I'm digging into whether ARK also needs 7778 UDP (the raw socket port, always game port+1) alongside 7777 — this feels similar to the Valheim three-port issue, and since it's not forwarded I'm flagging it as needing live verification rather than a confirmed break. I'm also noting Project Zomboid likely needs both 16261 and 16262 UDP forwarded (across B41 and B42), but only one appears open.

content.content:
/**
 * Team invitations: consent tokens, plus who is entitled to see whom.
 *
 * WHY THIS MODULE NO LONGER EXPORTS `requireArea`
 * ----------------------------------------------
 * It used to export `requireArea(orgId, area)` — a page guard for "org-scoped
 * dashboard pages". There were none: `requireArea` had zero call sites in the
 * repo (AUDIT-24H rec. 47, QA-PRELAUNCH P1-19), `memberCanAccessHref` was
 * referenced only from its own docblock, and `Membership.areas` was write-only.
 * Meanwhile the Team UI rendered a checkbox per dashboard area and reported
 * "Access updated." So an owner who unticked everything except Invoices was
 * shown a restriction that no loader, action or route ever consulted. That is
 * the same defect class as the fake SSL certs and the migration that logged 4/4
 * with six domains dark, and it is the more dangerous shape of it: a security
 * control that reports success while enforcing nothing.
 *
 * Wiring it up for real would mean org-scoping every dashboard loader and every
 * server action that touches a server, domain, volume, invoice or ticket — none
 * of which live in this module's blast radius. A half-wired version (nav hidden,
 * loaders open) is strictly worse than none, because hiding a nav item looks
 * like enforcement. So the area system is deleted rather than faked, and this
 * module now carries the two things teams genuinely need in order to be safe.
 *
 * 1. INVITE TOKENS (consent). `inviteMember` used to create a Membership
 *    outright — the invitee never agreed to anything — and the team page then
 *    handed the inviter every co-member's `userId` and email. That is precisely
 *    the identity feed that made the unauthenticated 2FA oracle
 *    (`verifyTotpForUser`, QA-PRELAUNCH P0-2) targetable at a named account:
 *    type a victim's email, get back their internal id. Membership now requires
 *    the invitee to click Accept while signed in as the invited address.
 *
 * 2. `canAdministerOrg` — the single definition of "may administer membership",
 *    used both to authorise mutations and to decide whether a viewer is
 *    entitled to co-members' email addresses.
 *
 * Plain server-side module (no "use server"), so both the server actions and the
 * accept page can import these helpers. Nothing here is client-safe.
 */
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { EncryptJWT, jwtDecrypt } from "jose";
 * Every actor is verified to hold a Membership of the required role in the
 * target org before any mutation runs, so a hand-crafted request can't touch
 * an org the caller doesn't belong to.
 *
 * WHAT A MEMBERSHIP ACTUALLY GRANTS (be precise — this used to be overstated):
 * visibility of the org roster, and, for OWNER/ADMIN, the right to invite,
 * re-role and remove members. It grants NOTHING ELSE. Servers, domains,
 * volumes, game servers, billing and invoices all remain scoped to the account
 * that owns them; no loader or action anywhere joins Membership to a resource.
 * The per-member "dashboard areas" control that used to sit on this page has
 * been removed rather than left in place: `Membership.areas` was written, echoed
 * back as saved, and read by nothing, so an owner who restricted a member to
 * Invoices was shown a restriction that did not exist. See lib/team-guard.ts for
 * why enforcing it for real is out of this change's reach, and the note rendered
 * in components/customer/TeamManager.tsx for what the customer is now told.
 *
 * CONSENT: `inviteMember` emails an invitation; only `acceptInvite`, run by the
 * invitee, creates a Membership. Nothing here can add a person to an org they
 * did not agree to join — see lib/team-guard.ts for the full rationale (it is
 * what fed the 2FA oracle, QA-PRELAUNCH P0-2).
 *
 * STILL OUT OF SCOPE: shared billing (org wallet / invoices) and members
 * inheriting access to shared servers. Deliberately absent, not half-built.
 */

const ROLES = ["OWNER", "ADMIN", "MEMBER", "BILLING"] as const;
type OrgRole = (typeof ROLES)[number];

function isRole(v: string): v is OrgRole {
  return (ROLES as readonly string[]).includes(v);
}

content.thinking:
Since there are no CLAUDE_BUILD jobs, I should skip that detail and instead note the gating on the customer's own API key. I'm now working through the precise list of orderable families with active GamePlans, starting to enumerate them from the gameplans file.

Continuing the enumeration, I count 42 total families. I also want to check structural details like image tagging conventions—most use `:latest` or untagged images except for a handful pinned to specific versions, which means two customers on the same family could end up running different image versions since images pull at provision time, creating risk if an upstream image introduces a breaking change.

Beyond that, I'm flagging several maintainer risk cases: didstopia/rust-server and didstopia/stationeers-server appear unmaintained or broken, several ARK and legacy game images haven't been updated in years, and a few smaller community images (Nightingale, Conan Exiles, Space Engineers, The Isle) come with explicit experimental or maintenance warnings. I'm weighing whether I can verify these via an external fetch within my read-only, time-bounded constraints.

For the game-specific setup review, Rust looks fine with its RCON port mapped and auto-updating install, though the Rust+ companion app port isn't exposed. Valheim checks out, and Palworld's player count setting seems fine but might need to match a player-cap schema. I'm also noting approximate disk sizes against plan allocations, starting with CS2's roughly 60-66GB footprint against the 100GB plan, while flagging that the health-check and chown permission issue is still an open blocker.

Moving through the other games, ARK Survival Evolved's ~23GB install fits its 40GB plan reasonably, though mods and saves make it tight, and ARK Survival Ascended's 13-15GB install against a 70GB plan is comfortable. Project Zomboid is messier — the 8GB tier's 25GB allocation is actually smaller than the 6GB tier's 30GB, which seems like an inconsistency from an earlier "entry tier fix," and I'm trying to reconcile how disk resizing during tier upgrades interacts with the base plan's disk allocation.

For the shooters, 7 Days to Die's roughly 12-15GB install fits its 35GB plan fine, but I'm less certain about Killing Floor 2 — its dedicated server might need around 15GB, which combined with OS and Docker overhead could make the 20GB plan uncomfortably tight, so I'm flagging that for verification. TF2's install is smaller and its 30GB plan works after their earlier correction, while Left 4 Dead 2's 10-13GB footprint against a 20GB plan also needs checking. I'm now trying to recall how large a Squad dedicated server install actually is, since I believe it runs notably bigger than these other titles.

Going through the rest of the roster — Mordhau, Conan, Space Engineers, The Isle, Satisfactory, Enshrouded, Soulmask, Stationeers, Nightingale, Icarus, Dragonwilds, Eco, Empyrion, Sandstorm, and Barotrauma — most seem to fit comfortably within their assigned disk plans based on typical install sizes, though Stationeers' known 13.3GB footprint on a 20GB plan is tight and likely already broken elsewhere. For Bedrock, I'm noting that even though the server itself is small, running it on a bare 1GB disk plan alongside the OS and Docker overhead seems questionable.

I'm flagging that Claude Code CLI is being pre-baked onto every game server VM regardless of type, which wastes disk space on the smallest plans — a minor issue but worth noting. On the RAM side, I'm more concerned: Rust's 4GB plan versus its 8GB template minimum is a real risk, CS2's 2GB plan is below its 4GB template minimum, and Minecraft's default 2G heap setting on a 2GB total RAM plan looks like a guaranteed out-of-memory situation since the JVM heap alone would consume the entire VM's memory.

Given itzg's default JVM settings and the overhead from Ubuntu, docker, and the log shipper, a 2GB Minecraft VM will almost certainly swap or crash — I want to flag this as high risk and verify whether there's actual evidence of failures on this tier, plus check the 1GB tier too.

I'm also noting some secondary issues: Palworld's player count config versus its tier limits isn't critical, CS2's GSLT automation for Steam Game Server Login Tokens looks fine, and DST correctly requires a token at checkout. But Sunkenland has a real bug — the worldGuid parameter is required at checkout but never actually gets wired into the server, so all Sunkenland instances end up sharing the same hardcoded GUID instead of the customer's requested one.

Dragonwilds' OWNER_ID looks properly wired through. Now I'm digging into NAT port forwarding gaps — ARK, Project Zomboid, and a few others seem fine, but The Forest and Sons of the Forest both rely on Steam's server browser for discovery (via their query ports) since neither supports direct IP connect, and the current join port configuration only forwards the game port, not the query port. That means NAT servers for these two games are likely undiscoverable or unjoinable as currently configured.

Sons of the Forest also needs its blob sync port for save syncing, which isn't forwarded — another likely breakage. Squad is the biggest issue though: it has no direct-connect option for players at all, so without its query port forwarded it simply won't appear in the server browser, making it completely unjoinable.

I'm noting several other missing ports across the list — Satisfactory's UDP 7777, Conan's 7777/udp, The Isle's 7777/udp, and Stationeers' 27500/udp are all absent, while Killing Floor 2 only exposes its query port for browser listing.

Sandstorm may not support direct connect for clients unlike others; TF2's SourceTV port is optional, GMod's client port isn't needed server-side, and I'm continuing through Empyrion's port requirements.

The broader pattern I'm seeing: for NAT servers, only one join port gets forwarded per family (Valheim being the exception), but many games actually need a second port for query/beacon/discovery to be joinable or show up in server browsers. Since I marked this deliberately incomplete without live verification, and customers have no Networking UI to add forwards themselves, this gap becomes a real blocker for those games.

Almost all live game servers are NAT-based, so this affects the majority of customers, not an edge case. I should flag this as HIGH severity with a per-family breakdown needing verification. I'm also checking whether the game panel's Network section references dead "platform Networking controls," how HOSTNAME_CONNECT_FAMILIES subdomain selection works at checkout for the fifteen affected families, and whether the "Manage → Worlds" notification is delivered as an email or just in-app.

content.thinking:
I'm flagging two stale images that haven't been updated in over a year: the barotrauma server docker hasn't seen an update since March 2023 despite over 1,400 pulls, and the Don't Starve Together image is even older at April 2021 with over 6,000 pulls—though it likely self-updates the game via steamcmd at runtime even if the base image is abandoned.

Checking a few more borderline images: the space engineers Wine-based container might break on SE updates, and several others sit around 20 months stale. Pull counts for the smaller titles are quite low, and I'm noting a couple of ghcr-hosted images to skip for now since they're outside the main registry pattern.

Now I'm building out the per-family comparison matrix covering plans, disk/RAM minimums, port checks, settings wiring, RCON support, mod support, art assets, and marketplace page status across all 42 game families, starting with the RAM/disk data pulled from each game's plan config.

I'm going through each family one by one, checking abioticfactor's plan tiers and port forwarding, then ark's settings wiring gaps and untested workshop mod support, then arkasa's hardcoded admin password issue, moving into barotrauma next.

Now I'm looking at bedrock's disk-size quirks and its auto-update-on-restart behavior, then flagging conan's broken TCP port config and its server binary that fails to start entirely.

Moving to corekeeper, I'm noting a GAME_CONFIG failure hit a live customer and its mod system isn't installable, then examining cs2's RAM shortfall below template minimums, its RCON-only player management, unusable mod install path, and a setup script missing a chown that leaves the container writing into its layer.

For dragonwilds I see seed drift with no mods, dst has stale 2021 images with workshop mods and one live instance, and eco runs an offline-flag entrypoint override whose implications for player auth and server browser visibility I'm still working through.

Moving on, empyrion has unforwarded UDP ports 30001-30003, enshrouded looks fine, and factorio is stuck on a stable image tag that never gets re-pulled — meaning the server never actually updates while clients on newer versions can't join, which is worth flagging. Gmod has several wired settings missing (gslt_token, workshop_collection, passwords) and its gamemode variants are being ignored entirely.

Continuing through icarus (query port not forwarded, variants ignored), kf2 (missing hero art, query port issue, large install size vs 20GB allocation), l4d2 (workshop mods, partial wiring), and minecraft, which has a notable gap between deploy-time wiring (2/17 fields) and what actually gets applied at runtime (17 fields) — plus unvalidated heap vs RAM sizing.

Now checking mordhau (mod_io mods not installable), necesse (looks fine), nightingale (ADMINPASSWORD not wired, experimental save-loss risk noted in README), palworld (mods restricted to Windows only), and projectzomboid — which has several real problems: non-monotonic disk sizing across plans, branch variants ignored since SERVER_BRANCH is blank, wrong dataRoot pointing at game binaries instead of the world archive, an unforwarded UDP port, and a live server that's been crash-looping since September 21st.

Continuing through rust (4GB plan undersized versus template minimum, RCON deferred, mods working via uMod), sandstorm and sdtd (both fully unwired), satisfactory (UDP game port and 8888/tcp unforwarded, likely unjoinable via NAT), sonsoftheforest (ports unforwarded, variants ignored), soulmask (fully wired and fine), spaceengineers (stale 2023 image, ports unwired), and now looking at squad's port forwarding gaps.

Moving on to stationeers (broken doc image but still orderable), sunkenland (worldGuid mismatch causing shared world state), terraria (settings ignored, image never re-pulled), tf2 (mostly wired, needs workshop auth), theforest (ports unforwarded, config-only archive), and theisle where Game.ini apparently can't be auto-generated since the schema gives it no write target.

I'm also noting more port-forwarding gaps for unturned, vintagestory, and vrising, plus ignored variant options across several games, and flagging that HOSTNAME_CONNECT families need a subdomain at checkout. There's also a UI quirk where the Mods tab appears even for families with zero catalog entries, showing a generic "curated per game" message instead of hiding the tab.

For cs2 specifically, I'm checking plan counts and noticing RAM sized well below the template minimum for higher slot counts. I'm also tracing how the RCON port forward on 27015/tcp is created and retracted during provisioning on non-primary nodes, and finding that a failed provision from 09-16 left that forward published because the retraction step was skipped when the error was thrown early.

This confirms a real code-level bug: the cleanup path for failed provisions never removes the check-port forward, leaving RCON exposed on non-primary nodes when provisioning fails. I'm tracing the exact lines where the forward gets allocated, where the throw happens, and where cleanup runs but doesn't touch forwards, and confirming the live cs2 row is indeed on a non-primary node with only the 27015/tcp forward still active — consistent with this failure mode.

Checking the Overview's billing link, it just points to a read-only renewables list with no renew or auto-renew controls, and the Suspended banner tells users to contact support instead of linking to the pay flow that already exists on the billing page — both medium-severity gaps.

Now I'm looking at VM power controls for game servers: Start is only enabled when the VM is STOPPED, but the game control action always returns an error saying the VM must be running, since there's no VM-start branch for games. I'm trying to figure out how a game VM could even end up STOPPED, and a failed backup restore leaving the VM powered off seems like the likely path.

That's a realistic and high-severity scenario since the customer would be stuck needing support.
